argument_summary: The admissible record supports only a narrow, qualified certification position. Aggregate readiness is met, there were no severity-one rehearsal incidents, and staged rollout, rollback, and monitoring are in place. That does not make rollout controls a substitute for the policy predicate. The supportable position is narrower: certification is defensible only if treated as qualified and tied to explicit pre-launch model-card disclosure of the known HR benefits enrollment limitation, with deployment monitoring as a secondary control. The audit concern is valid to the extent the packet should not be read as claiming that compliance is already complete on rollout controls alone.
claims_about_business_cost: No claim is made that business cost changes the policy standard. The practical governance point is narrower: where aggregate readiness is otherwise passing and the remaining weakness is known and documentable, a qualified certification with explicit disclosure and monitoring avoids unnecessary escalation while keeping the decision aligned to the written policy path.
claims_about_policy: The policy does not permit treating a 9% rollout, rollback switch, or monitoring dashboard as sufficient by themselves while the affected HR benefits enrollment use case remains exposed. The same policy does allow certification on a qualified basis if the material limitation is disclosed before launch, because disclosure is the stated route when the issue is unresolved and there is no approved risk acceptance. Public guidance on model cards and deployment monitoring supports that disclosure-and-monitoring structure, but does not replace the internal requirement.
concessions: The current admissible record does not show an approved risk acceptance specific to the exposed HR benefits enrollment segment.
The current admissible record does not show that the rollout excludes the affected use case.
The packet should not claim that rollout controls alone satisfy compliance.
The record, as presented, supports identifying disclosure as required, not asserting that disclosure has already been evidenced.
